quotes.quote: Bidri ware is a famous handicraft of Bidar District.
Bidriware is an alloy ofzinc , copper and other non ferrous metals. Pretty designs are engtaved on it and there after inlaid with pure silver ware.
The technique consists of casting objects from a high-zinc alloy and then inlaying them with silver or brass, or a combination of both.
The technique takes its name from the city of Bidar, in present day Karnataka, where it is thought to have originated
The art with silver is called Bidriware-so called after the name of the old city of Bidar
The very name "Bidri' is derived from Bidar
The craft ofBidriware is a kind of damascene work.
It is a system of orna mentation consisting of encrusting one metal on the other.
Bidriware is a special type of work called Damascening in silver.
The contrast between the black oxidized background and lustrous silver inlay gives a beauty to the Bidri ware.
The inlays contrast strikingly with the matt black patina of the vessel.
Bidri is a technique known only in the Indian subcontinent
This metalwork as well as the technique to produce it are found in India alone.
Bidar remains one of the chief centres of bidriware production in the country, alongside Hyderabad in present-day Telangana.
Today, Bidri is produced only in two centres in India: Bidar and Hyderabad.
It was introduced in Bidar about 400 years ago by King Ahmed Shah Wali Bhamani.
Its name is derived from Bidar where the skill in this art was developed during time of Ahmed Shah Bahamani (1422 A.D.- 1436 A.D)
The history of bidriware is said to have begun with the reign of Ahmed Shah Al Wali Baihmani.
Ahmed Shah Al Wali Baihmani (1422-1436), the ninth king of the Baihmani dynasty ruled for a period of 13 years and was a great patron of the arts.

Its origins are unknown, but surviving pieces date from the late 16th or early 17th century.
The earliest pieces of bidri date from the early 17th century, when production is thought to have been only in centres such as Bidar and Hyderadabad in the Deccan sultanates.
The earliest evidence of a bidriware object comes from a Deccani painting dated to c. 1625, in which an officer of African descent is seen smoking a hookah made in the bidri technique.
No examples of bidri dating to the 15th or 16th centuries have been found in paintings or literature, thus making one sceptical if bidri should still be related to the 15th century or not.
The earliest reference of bidri ware is in Chahar Gulshan, a history of India written in Persian in 1759, which in turn is based on a work of 1720

By the late eighteenth century, the technique had spread to the Muslim courts of Purnia (in present-day Bihar) and Murshidabad (in present-day Bengal), and by the nineteenth century, to Lucknow (in present-day Uttar Pradesh).
It gained such popularity that working centres came to be opent'd at Murshidabad in Bengal, Lucknow in Uttar Pn,desh and Purniah in Bihar.
By the early 19th century, bidri started to be produced in other parts of India-Lucknow, Purnea and Murshidabad.
The technique flourished in Bidar and Hyderabad between the sixteenth and nineteenth century and regularly appeared in Deccan paintings from the seventeenth century onwards.
Bidriware from the region was also exported to the Mughal court, Rajput courts of Rajasthan and Maratha kingdoms.
The art form was also extensively patronised by the Asaf Jahi Dynasty that ruled over the Hyderabad State between the eighteenth and twentieth century.
From the early 18th century to the mid-20th century, the bidri industry flourished under the Asaf Jahi rulers.
Many artisans from Bidar migrated to Hyderabad, which was the new capital of the Deccan. The art started to flourish in Hyderabad.
At the time of Re-organisation of States in the year 1956 Bidar was included in Mysore State.
So, many of them chose to migrate to Hyderabad City and came there in the years 1956 and 1957.
Most artisans moved to Hyderabad in search of better livelihoods as it remained a hub for trade.

The varieties of workmanship of the designs consist of tarkashi (inlay of wire), tainishan (inlay of sheet), zarnishan (low relief), zarbuland (high relief) and aftabi (cut out designs on overlaid metal sheet).
Tarkashi is nothing but plain wire work. Grooves for the required design are made on the surface of the object.
Tarkashi is simply plain wire work and thus appears to be more intricate with fine lines.
Teh nashin refers to 'thick inlay of gold or silver in deep engravings on a baser metal surface' (Sen 1983:37).
The designs are flushed with the surface of the metal without any relief.
Aftabi, also known as mehatabi, refers to silver inlay on the background while the designs appear to be in black.
The Aftabi also known as Mehatabi work refers to pieces that portray a reversal - the silver seems to form the base while the designs seems to be in black.
In bidri it is done using a 'zar buland' where silver is inlaid over a lead pad so that the pattern stands up from the surface (Stronge 1985:11).
In the zarbuland technique, the silver is inlaid over a lead pad and is then incised with motifs or gold overlay, leading to a high-relief effect.
The margin or rim of each is bent over and the cavity thus formed is filled with a piece of soft lead.
A distinctive inlay style, called zarbuland (high-relief inlaying), was developed in Lucknow.
The inlay with high relief-zarbuland or zarnishan (creating a raised effect)-comes from Lucknow.
Ganga-Yamuna style - where gold and silver are used side-by-side for inlays, though this is now taken to mean an inlay of two or more metals
The pattern's true meaning of using two specified metals-gold and silver, today translates to the use of any two or more metals for inlay.
And after the final colouring of the article, gold is inlaid. This is because gold is a softer metal and it tends to fall out during the process of buffing and polishing.
The most famous of Tarkashi designs is Phooljhadi (fountain).
Star work, commonly known as phooljhadi work, is also an example of tarkashi.
The most beautiful and best known pattern, the 'Mughal poppy flower motif' is said to be introduced around 1740 and has since been used in bidri extensively.
In the eighteenth century, a popular motif, also derived from Mughal art, was the poppy flower, which was used extensively.
By the mid-nineteenth century, as the quality and use of the poppy motif declined, the kothmir (coriander) leaf motif became popular, and its variations were used until the twentieth century.
The kothmiri design which is seen 1850 onwards, appears to get more prominent and continues until the 20th century.

Highly conventionalised patterns, ashrafi-ki booti or teenpatti-ki-booti, stars, vine creepers and stylized poppy plant with flower, single bloom or whole plant in various shapes, mostly in medallion form or mango shape, are amongst those which can be traced back to Persian influence.
Fish-shaped spice boxes are common to Lucknow and Bidar, but articles ornamented with fish designs are special to Lucknow only.
In Lucknow, the double-fish insignia of the Nawabs of Awadh was a common motif.
